Floating-point addition is not associative because modern hardware represents real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, changing the grouping of a sum does not change its value: adding three numbers in either order produces the same mathematical result. Floating-point hardware, however, must round most intermediate results to the nearest representable value. Because rounding occurs after each operation, changing the order of operations changes which intermediate values are rounded and can therefore change the final result.

The effect is especially visible when numbers have very different magnitudes. Before two floating-point values are added, their significands must be aligned according to their exponents. If one value is much smaller than the other, some or all of its significant bits may be shifted away. Adding a tiny value to a large value can thus leave the large value unchanged, even though repeatedly accumulating many such tiny values should eventually have a measurable effect. If the tiny values are added together first, their combined sum may become large enough to affect the larger value. Cancellation between nearly equal positive and negative values can further amplify the relative impact of rounding errors.

Large matrix multiplications contain many dot products, each of which requires a reduction over numerous products. Mathematical notation treats the terms as a single exact sum, but an implementation must select a reduction order. A serial implementation might accumulate terms from left to right. A multicore CPU may divide the terms among threads, compute partial sums, and then combine those sums. A GPU often uses tree-shaped reductions across many lanes. Different tile sizes, thread schedules, vector widths, compiler optimizations, and distributed communication patterns can all produce different groupings.

Consequently, two implementations can use the same input matrices and the same nominal floating-point format yet produce results that differ in their low-order bits. The differences are usually small, but they may grow for long dot products, poorly conditioned problems, or computations involving substantial cancellation. They can also propagate through later nonlinear or iterative calculations and eventually cause visibly different outcomes.

Fused multiply-add instructions add another source of variation because they compute a product and addition with a single final rounding, whereas separate multiplication and addition usually round twice. This is often more accurate, but it may not match hardware or compiler settings that do not use fusion. Reproducibility therefore requires more than fixing inputs and random seeds. It may require deterministic reduction trees, consistent instruction choices, controlled compiler settings, or specialized reproducible summation algorithms. Even then, bitwise reproducibility can carry performance costs, since high-performance matrix multiplication relies heavily on parallelism and flexible reduction ordering.
